analysis.one_liner: Applies the Social Security payroll tax to all wages and boosts annual cost-of-living raises for seniors.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee with two cosponsors and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would change Social Security in two main ways. It would base annual cost-of-living increases on an inflation index that tracks what people 62 and older actually buy, which typically rises faster than the index used today. And starting in 2025 it would gradually apply the 12.4% Social Security payroll tax to all wage and self-employment income, phasing out the current cap on taxed earnings by 2031, while crediting high earners only a small extra benefit for the extra taxes they pay.
analysis.who_benefits: Current and future Social Security retirees, survivors, and disability beneficiaries, whose annual cost-of-living adjustments would better match seniors' actual expenses. The added tax revenue from high earners would also extend the program's solvency, protecting benefits for everyone who depends on them.

how_it_helps.text: The bill directs the Bureau of Labor Statistics to publish a Consumer Price Index for Elderly Consumers and uses it to compute Social Security cost-of-living increases, and it ensures any resulting benefit increase does not reduce SSI or Medicaid benefits.

Starting in 2025 the bill applies the Social Security payroll tax to a rising share of wages and self-employment income above the contribution and benefit base — 86% in 2025, declining yearly until all such income is taxed after 2030.

It credits high earners a small benefit increase for earnings above the cap (3% on a first tier and 0.25% beyond that), so the new tax revenue primarily strengthens the program's finances rather than raising benefits for high earners.

analysis.who_pays: Higher earners — employees, employers, and self-employed people — would pay the 12.4% combined Social Security payroll tax on wages and self-employment income above the current taxable maximum, which they largely do not pay today. High earners would receive only a small extra benefit in return.

drawbacks.text: High earners and self-employed professionals would face a substantial new tax on income above the taxable cap, with only a small fraction credited back in benefits — an honest supporter would acknowledge this is a redistribution designed to shore up the trust fund, not a benefit-neutral change.

The bill taxes only wage and self-employment income, not investment income, so much of the income of the wealthiest households would remain untouched while earned-income taxes rise — a common criticism of cap-lifting proposals.

Using the elderly price index would raise every future cost-of-living adjustment, increasing long-run program costs at the same time the bill raises revenue; opponents of expanding Social Security taxes would argue the combined cost to high-income workers is too high.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the tens of millions of people who depend on Social Security, the bill offers a modestly higher annual benefit increase and stronger program financing, paid for almost entirely by the top slice of earners, who would pay full payroll taxes on income they currently stop paying at the cap. The main honest objection is that it leaves untaxed the investment income of the very wealthiest and raises costs on small-business owners and high-wage professionals, but on balance the trade favors ordinary beneficiaries.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in late July 2024 and sent to the Senate Finance Committee, which never took it up, and it died there when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Mazie Hirono introduced the bill on July 31, 2024, joined by two Democratic cosponsors.
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance, where it received no further action.
The 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, so the bill expired in committee without a hearing, a markup, or any vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: High earners who would have paid the payroll tax on all their wages are better off, since the bill died; the Social Security financing gap it was meant to narrow remains unaddressed by this bill.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: High earners who would have paid the tax

for.name: Sen. Mazie Hirono
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and introduced it in the Senate.

for.name: Sens. Jeff Merkley and Tina Smith
for.what_they_did: Joined as cosponsors when the bill was introduced.

against.name: Senate Committee on Finance
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Sen. Ron Wyden
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken; all three supporters were Senate Democrats and no Republican cosponsored, so the bill never drew a recorded opposition.

industries.industry: High-income earners (wages and self-employment income above the Social Security cap)
industries.note: They would pay the full 12.4% Social Security tax on earnings above the cap, phased in from 2025 to 2031, while receiving only a small benefit credit in return. The revenue would strengthen the program that most retirees depend on.
Employers pay half of Social Security payroll taxes, so removing the cap raises their tax on high salaries as well. The cost is borne at the top of the wage scale.

industries.industry: Self-employed professionals and small-business owners with high earnings
industries.note: The bill applies the same phase-in to net self-employment earnings above the cap, so solo practitioners and owners of profitable businesses face the increase without an employer sharing it.
